His heart is a hanging lute;
As soon as it is touched, it sounds.
—De Béranger.

Through the whole of a dull, dark, silent autumn day, with clouds hanging oppressively low in the sky, I had been riding alone through an exceptionally dreary stretch of country. At last, as evening shadows gathered, I came within sight of the melancholy House of Usher. I cannot say why, but at my first glimpse of the building, a feeling of unbearable gloom spread through my spirit. I say unbearable because there was none of the half-pleasurable, poetic feeling with which we usually receive even the bleakest natural scenes of desolation or terror. I looked at the scene before me: at the house itself and the plain features of its grounds; at the bleak walls and vacant, eye-like windows; at a few clumps of overgrown sedge and a few white trunks of decaying trees. My soul sank into a depression that I can compare to no earthly sensation better than an opium reveller’s awakening from a dream: the bitter return to everyday life, the hideous falling away of the veil. My heart turned icy, sank and sickened. My thoughts were utterly dreary, and no effort of imagination could force them into anything sublime. What was it, I paused to wonder, that so unnerved me as I looked at the House of Usher? The mystery was insoluble. I could not grasp the shadowy fancies crowding upon me as I considered it. I had to fall back on an unsatisfactory conclusion. Certain arrangements of very simple natural objects undoubtedly have the power to affect us like this, but understanding that power lies beyond our depth. Perhaps, I reflected, simply rearranging the details of the scene, the elements of the picture, would change or even destroy its power to make me sad. Acting on this idea, I guided my horse to the steep edge of a black, lurid little lake lying beside the house, its lustrous surface undisturbed. I gazed down, but with an even more piercing shudder than before, at the rearranged, upside-down images of the grey sedge, the ghastly tree trunks, and the vacant, eye-like windows.

Yet I intended to stay for several weeks in this mansion of gloom. Its owner, Roderick Usher, had been one of my close companions in boyhood, though many years had passed since we last met. Recently, however, a letter from him had reached me in a distant part of the country. Its desperate urgency left me no choice but to answer in person. The written letter showed nervous agitation. He spoke of acute physical illness, of a mental disorder that weighed upon him, and of his earnest wish to see me as his best, indeed his only personal friend. He hoped my cheerful company might bring some relief to his illness. It was the way he said all this and much more, the apparent heartfelt sincerity of his request, that left me no room to hesitate. I immediately obeyed what I still considered a very strange summons.

Although we had been intimate friends as boys, I really knew little about him. He had always been extremely and habitually reserved. I did know that his very ancient family had been noted, for as long as anyone could remember, for an unusually sensitive temperament. Over the centuries this had found expression in many works of elevated art. More recently it had appeared in repeated acts of generous but quiet charity, and in a passionate devotion to the complexities of music, perhaps even more than to its established and easily recognised beauties. I had also learned a remarkable fact. Ancient and honoured though the Usher family’s trunk was, it had never put out any lasting branch. In other words, the entire family lay in a single direct line of descent, and, apart from very slight and temporary variations, always had. I turned this over in my mind as I considered how perfectly the character of the property matched the family’s reputed character. I wondered what influence one might have had on the other over the long centuries. Perhaps it was this lack of descendants in side branches, and the resulting unbroken passage of both estate and name from father to son, that had eventually made the two indistinguishable. The estate’s original name had merged into the curious, ambiguous name “House of Usher”. To the country people who used it, this seemed to mean both the family and the family mansion.

As I have said, my rather childish experiment of looking into the lake had only deepened my first strange impression. There is no doubt that noticing how rapidly my superstition was growing—for why should I not call it that?—did more than anything to make it grow faster. I have long known that this is the contradictory law governing all feelings founded on terror. Perhaps this alone explains the strange fancy that entered my mind when I raised my eyes from the house’s reflection to the house itself. It was so ridiculous that I mention it only to show the vivid force of the sensations oppressing me. I had worked on my imagination until I actually believed that an atmosphere peculiar to the mansion, its grounds and their immediate surroundings hung over them all. It had nothing in common with the air of the heavens. It had risen like a stench from the decayed trees, the grey wall and the silent lake: a diseased, mysterious vapour, dull, sluggish, barely visible and leaden in colour.

Shaking off what must have been a dream, I examined the building’s actual appearance more closely. Its chief feature seemed to be its extreme age. The centuries had badly discoloured it. Tiny fungi spread across its whole exterior, hanging from the eaves in a fine, tangled web. Yet this was not accompanied by any exceptional structural ruin. None of the masonry had fallen. The way its parts still fitted perfectly together seemed wildly at odds with the crumbling condition of the individual stones. It reminded me strongly of old woodwork that has rotted for years in a neglected vault, undisturbed by any breath of outside air, while still appearing deceptively whole. Beyond this sign of extensive decay, however, the structure showed little evidence of instability. Perhaps a careful observer might have noticed a barely visible crack running from the front of the roof, zigzagging down the wall until it disappeared into the sullen waters of the lake.

Noticing these things, I rode across a short causeway to the house. A waiting servant took my horse, and I entered the hall’s Gothic archway. From there, a valet with a stealthy step led me silently through many dark, winding passages towards his master’s studio. Much that I encountered on the way somehow heightened the vague feelings I have already described. The carved ceilings, the sombre wall tapestries, the ebony-black floors, and the fantastic, ghostlike displays of arms that rattled as I strode past were all things, or like things, I had known since infancy. I readily admitted how familiar they were. Yet I wondered at the unfamiliar fancies these ordinary sights stirred in me. On one staircase I met the family physician. His face seemed to combine mean cunning with perplexity. He greeted me nervously and passed on. The valet then threw open a door and brought me into his master’s presence.

The room was very large and high. Its windows were long, narrow and pointed, so far above the black oak floor that they were completely inaccessible from inside. Weak gleams of crimson light entered through the latticed panes, making the more prominent objects around me clear enough. But my eyes struggled in vain to reach the room’s distant corners or the recesses of its vaulted, intricately patterned ceiling. Dark hangings covered the walls. The furniture was plentiful, uncomfortable, antique and tattered. Many books and musical instruments lay scattered about, but brought no life to the scene. I felt I was breathing an atmosphere of sorrow. A harsh, deep, unrelieved gloom hung over everything and filled it all.

As I entered, Usher rose from a sofa where he had been lying stretched out. He greeted me with lively warmth that at first seemed exaggerated, like the forced effort of a bored man of the world. But one look at his face convinced me that he was perfectly sincere. We sat down. For several moments he said nothing, and I looked at him with a mixture of pity and awe. Surely no man had ever changed so terribly in so short a time as Roderick Usher! I could scarcely accept that the pale being before me was the companion of my early boyhood. Yet his face had always been remarkable. He had a corpse-like complexion; large, liquid eyes of incomparable brightness; thin, very pale lips with a curve of surpassing beauty; and a delicately shaped Hebrew nose, but with nostrils unusually broad for that form. His finely moulded chin, through its lack of prominence, suggested a lack of moral strength. His hair was finer and softer than a web. Together with the extraordinary breadth above his temples, these features formed a face not easily forgotten. Now, simply by intensifying their dominant character and their usual expression, they had changed him so much that I doubted who I was speaking to. Above all, the now ghastly pallor of his skin and astonishing brilliance of his eyes startled and even awed me. His silken hair had been allowed to grow completely untended. With its wild, gossamer texture, it floated rather than fell about his face. Even with an effort, I could not connect its intricate, fantastic appearance with any idea of ordinary humanity.

I was immediately struck by something disjointed and inconsistent in my friend’s manner. I soon discovered that it came from a series of weak, unsuccessful efforts to overcome his habitual trembling and extreme nervous agitation. I had been prepared for something of the kind, not only by his letter, but by memories of certain boyhood traits and by conclusions I had drawn from his peculiar physique and temperament. He was lively one moment, sullen the next. His voice changed rapidly from a trembling uncertainty, when his natural vitality seemed completely suspended, to a kind of forceful brevity. Then his speech was abrupt, weighty, unhurried and hollow-sounding: a heavy, self-controlled, perfectly modulated utterance from the throat, such as one hears from a hopeless drunkard or an incurable opium eater in moments of the most intense excitement.

In this way he spoke of the purpose of my visit, his earnest wish to see me, and the comfort he expected me to bring. At some length, he explained what he believed his illness to be. It was, he said, an evil rooted in his constitution and his family, and he despaired of finding a remedy. A mere nervous disorder, he immediately added, which would undoubtedly soon pass. It showed itself in a host of unnatural sensations. Some of those he described both interested and bewildered me, although perhaps his choice of words and manner of telling contributed to the effect. He suffered greatly from a morbid sharpness of the senses. He could bear only the blandest food and wear only clothes of certain textures. The scent of every flower oppressed him. Even faint light tortured his eyes. Only particular sounds, produced by stringed instruments, failed to fill him with horror.

I found him enslaved to an extraordinary kind of terror. “I shall die,” he said. “I must die in this miserable folly. In this way, this way and no other, I shall be lost. I dread future events, not for themselves, but for their consequences. I shudder at the thought of any incident, however trivial, that might affect this unbearable agitation of my soul. I do not really hate danger, except for its ultimate effect: terror. In this unnerved, pitiable state, I feel that sooner or later the time must come when I lose both life and reason in some struggle with the grim phantom, FEAR.”

From time to time, through broken, ambiguous hints, I learned another strange feature of his mental state. He was bound by certain superstitious beliefs about the house he lived in, which he had not ventured outside for many years. He believed in an influence whose supposed power he described too vaguely for me to repeat here. He said that certain peculiarities in the mere shape and substance of his family mansion had gained control over his spirit through his long exposure to them. The physical nature of the grey walls and turrets, and of the dim lake into which they all looked down, had finally brought about this effect on his inner life.

He admitted, though hesitantly, that much of the peculiar gloom afflicting him had a more natural and far more tangible cause. His dearly loved sister had been seriously ill for a long time and was evidently approaching death. She had been his only companion for many years, his last and only relative on earth. “Her death,” he said with a bitterness I can never forget, “would leave me—hopeless and frail—the last of the ancient Usher family.” As he spoke, Lady Madeline, for that was her name, passed slowly through a distant part of the room and disappeared without noticing me. I watched her in complete astonishment, mixed with dread, yet could not account for these feelings. A numbing stupor oppressed me as my eyes followed her retreating steps. At last a door closed behind her. Instinctively and eagerly, I looked towards her brother’s face. But he had buried it in his hands. All I could see was that his wasted fingers had become far paler than usual, and that many passionate tears trickled between them.

Lady Madeline’s illness had long defeated her physicians’ skill. Their unusual diagnosis was a settled apathy, a gradual wasting of the body, and frequent but brief attacks of a partly cataleptic kind. Until now she had steadily resisted the pressure of her illness and had not finally taken to her bed. But as evening closed in on the day I arrived, she gave way to the destroyer’s exhausting power. Her brother told me this that night in indescribable agitation. I learned that my glimpse of her would therefore probably be my last: at least while she lived, I would see Lady Madeline no more.

For several days afterwards, neither Usher nor I mentioned her name. During that time I earnestly tried to relieve my friend’s melancholy. We painted and read together, or I listened as if in a dream to the wild improvisations of his speaking guitar. As our friendship grew closer and closer, he let me more freely into the recesses of his spirit. And the more he did so, the more bitterly I saw how useless it was to try to cheer his mind. Darkness seemed an actual quality inherent in it, pouring onto every object in the moral and physical universe in one unceasing radiation of gloom.

I will always carry the memory of the many solemn hours I spent alone with the master of the House of Usher. Yet I could not convey the exact nature of the studies or pursuits in which he involved me or led the way. His excited, deeply disordered imagination cast a sulphurous glow over everything. His long, improvised laments will ring in my ears for ever. Among other things, I painfully remember a strange distortion and expansion of the wild melody of Von Weber’s last waltz. His elaborate imagination brooded over his paintings, which grew, touch by touch, into vague forms. I shuddered at them all the more intensely because I did not know why I shuddered. Vividly as their images now stand before me, I could express no more than a small part of them in written words. The utter simplicity, the bareness of his designs, seized and overawed the attention. If any mortal ever painted an idea, it was Roderick Usher. For me, at least, in the circumstances then surrounding me, the pure abstractions this hypochondriac put on canvas produced an unbearable intensity of awe. I have never felt a shadow of it while looking at Fuseli’s reveries, certainly vivid but too concrete.

One of my friend’s fantastic conceptions, less strictly abstract than the others, can be faintly suggested in words. A small painting showed the inside of an immensely long, rectangular vault or tunnel. Its walls were low, smooth and white, without a break or decoration. Certain additional details of the design conveyed the impression that this excavation lay at an immense depth beneath the earth. No opening could be seen anywhere along its vast length, nor any torch or other artificial source of light. Yet a flood of intense rays rolled through it, bathing everything in a ghastly, inappropriate splendour.

I have mentioned the morbid condition of his auditory nerve, which made all music intolerable to him except certain effects from stringed instruments. Perhaps the narrow limits he therefore imposed on his guitar playing largely accounted for the fantastic nature of his performances. But they could not explain the passionate ease of his improvisations. That ease, both in the notes and in the words of his wild musical fantasies—for he often accompanied himself with improvised rhyming verses—must have come, and did come, from the intense mental composure and concentration I have already described. It is found only in particular moments of the most intense, artificially induced excitement. I have easily remembered the words of one of these rhapsodies. Perhaps his performance struck me more forcibly because I thought I detected, in the hidden, mysterious current of its meaning, something I had not perceived before: Usher’s complete awareness that his lofty reason was tottering on her throne. The verses were called “The Haunted Palace”, and ran very nearly, if not exactly, as follows:

I.
In the greenest of our valleys,
Where good angels used to dwell,
Once a fair and stately palace—
A radiant palace—raised its head.
Within the kingdom ruled by Thought—
There it stood!
No seraph ever spread a wing
Over a building half so fair.

II.
Yellow banners, glorious, golden,
On its roof would float and flow;
(This—all this—was in the old
Time long ago)
And every gentle breeze that lingered,
On that sweet day,
Along the feathered, pale ramparts,
Departed as a winged fragrance.

III.
Wanderers in that happy valley
Through two shining windows saw
Spirits moving musically
To the rule of a well-tuned lute,
Around a throne, where seated
(Porphyrogene!)
In state befitting all his glory,
The ruler of the realm was seen.

IV.
And glowing all with pearl and ruby
Was the fair palace door,
Through which came flowing, flowing, flowing,
And sparkling evermore,
A troop of Echoes whose sweet duty
Was only to sing,
In voices of surpassing beauty,
The wit and wisdom of their king.

V.
But evil things, in robes of sorrow,
Attacked the monarch’s high position;
(Ah, let us mourn, for no tomorrow
Will dawn upon him, desolate!)
And, all around his home, the glory
That blushed and bloomed
Is only a dimly remembered story
Of old times buried in a tomb.

VI.
And travellers now within that valley,
Through the red-lit windows, see
Vast forms moving fantastically
To a discordant melody;
While, like a rapid, ghastly river,
Through the pale door,
A hideous throng rushes out for ever,
And laughs—but smiles no more.

I remember well how the suggestions in this ballad led our thoughts in a direction that revealed one of Usher’s opinions. I mention it less for its novelty—others have thought the same*—than for the stubbornness with which he defended it. In its general form, it was the belief that all plants can feel. But in his disordered imagination, the idea had grown bolder and, under certain conditions, extended to things without organic life. I have no words for the full extent of his conviction, or for the wholehearted intensity with which he gave himself to it. The belief was connected, as I have already hinted, with the grey stones of his ancestral home. He imagined that the necessary conditions for feeling had been fulfilled here by the way these stones were placed: by their arrangement, and that of the many fungi covering them and the decayed trees around them. Above all, he pointed to the long, undisturbed persistence of this arrangement and its duplication in the still lake. The evidence, the evidence that they could feel, lay, he said—and I started as he spoke—in the gradual but certain gathering of an atmosphere of their own around the waters and the walls. Its result, he added, could be found in the silent but insistent and terrible influence that had shaped his family’s destiny for centuries and made him what I now saw, what he was. Such opinions need no comment, and I shall make none.
* Watson, Dr. Percival, Spallanzani, and especially the Bishop of Landaff. See “Chemical Essays”, volume 5.

Our books, which for years had formed a large part of the invalid’s mental life, were, as one might expect, entirely in keeping with these fantastic ideas. Together we pored over Gresset’s Ververt and The Charterhouse; Machiavelli’s Belphegor; Swedenborg’s Heaven and Hell; Holberg’s Subterranean Voyage of Nicholas Klimm; the works on palmistry by Robert Flud, Jean D’Indaginé and De la Chambre; Tieck’s Journey into the Blue Distance; and Campanella’s City of the Sun. One favourite was a small octavo edition of the Manual of the Inquisitors, by the Dominican Eymeric de Gironne. There were also passages in Pomponius Mela about the ancient African satyrs and OEgipans over which Usher would sit dreaming for hours. His greatest delight, however, was an exceptionally rare and curious quarto book in Gothic type, the manual of a forgotten church: Vigils for the Dead According to the Choir of the Church of Mainz.

I could not help thinking of the wild ritual in this book, and its probable influence on the hypochondriac, when one evening he abruptly told me that Lady Madeline was dead. He then announced his intention of keeping her corpse in one of the many vaults within the building’s main walls for a fortnight before its final burial. The practical reason he gave for this strange procedure was one I did not feel free to challenge. As he told me, he had reached his decision because of the unusual nature of his sister’s illness, certain intrusive and eager inquiries by her doctors, and the isolated, exposed position of the family burial ground. I will not deny that, when I remembered the sinister face of the man I had met on the staircase on my first day, I had no wish to oppose what I considered nothing more than a harmless and by no means unnatural precaution.

At Usher’s request, I personally helped him prepare for the temporary entombment. Once the body was in its coffin, we two carried it alone to its resting place. The vault had been unopened for so long that our torches, half smothered by its oppressive air, gave us little chance to inspect it. It was small, damp, and had no opening through which light could enter. It lay deep and directly beneath the part of the house containing my own bedroom. Apparently, in remote feudal times it had served the worst purposes of a castle keep. Later it had been used to store gunpowder or some other highly flammable substance, for part of its floor and the whole inside of the long archway through which we entered were carefully lined with copper. The massive iron door had the same protection. Its immense weight made it grate unusually sharply as it turned on its hinges.

We placed our mournful burden on trestles in this region of horror. Then we partly moved aside the coffin lid, which had not yet been screwed down, and looked at its occupant’s face. For the first time, the striking resemblance between brother and sister caught my attention. Perhaps guessing my thoughts, Usher murmured a few words from which I learned that he and the dead woman were twins, and that they had always been linked in ways that could scarcely be understood. But we did not look at the dead woman for long, for we could not do so without awe. The illness that had entombed her in the prime of youth had left, as strictly cataleptic illnesses always do, the mockery of a faint blush on her breast and face, and that suspiciously lingering smile on her lips which is so terrible in death. We replaced the lid and screwed it down. After securing the iron door, we made our way with difficulty back to the rooms above, which were scarcely less gloomy.

Several days of bitter grief passed. Then a noticeable change came over my friend’s mental disorder. His usual manner disappeared. He neglected or forgot his normal activities. He wandered from room to room with hurried, uneven, aimless steps. His face had become, if possible, even more ghastly in its pallor, but all the brightness had gone out of his eyes. The occasional huskiness of his voice was no longer heard. Instead, a trembling quaver, as if of extreme terror, had become habitual. At times I thought his endlessly agitated mind was struggling with some oppressive secret, and that he was trying to find the courage to reveal it. At other times I had to put everything down to the inexplicable whims of madness. I saw him stare into emptiness for hours with the deepest attention, as though listening to an imaginary sound. It was no wonder his condition frightened me, that it infected me. Slowly but surely, I felt the wild influence of his fantastic yet powerful superstitions creeping over me.

I felt the full power of these emotions particularly when I went to bed late on the seventh or eighth night after Lady Madeline had been placed in the dungeon. Sleep never approached my bed as the hours dwindled and dwindled away. I tried to reason away the nervousness that controlled me. I tried to believe that much, perhaps all, of what I felt came from the bewildering effect of the room’s gloomy furnishings. Its dark, tattered hangings were twisted into motion by the breath of a rising storm. They swayed fitfully along the walls and rustled uneasily around the bed’s decorations. But my efforts were useless. An uncontrollable trembling gradually spread through my body. At last a nightmare demon of utterly groundless alarm seemed to sit upon my very heart. With a gasp and a struggle, I shook it off and raised myself on the pillows. I peered intently into the room’s deep darkness and listened, for no reason I can give except instinct, to certain low, indistinct sounds. They came at long intervals, during pauses in the storm, from somewhere I could not identify. An intense horror overwhelmed me, inexplicable but unbearable. I hurriedly put on my clothes, feeling that I would sleep no more that night, and tried to rouse myself from this pitiable state by pacing rapidly back and forth across the room.

After only a few turns, a light step on a neighbouring staircase caught my attention. I soon recognised Usher’s tread. A moment later he knocked gently at my door and came in carrying a lamp. As usual, his face was deathly pale. But his eyes also held a kind of mad hilarity, and his whole manner showed a hysteria he was plainly struggling to restrain. His appearance appalled me. Yet anything was better than the loneliness I had endured for so long, and I even welcomed his presence as a relief.

“And you haven’t seen it?” he said suddenly, after looking around in silence for several moments. “Then you haven’t seen it? But wait! You shall.” As he spoke, he carefully shielded his lamp, hurried to one of the windows, and threw it wide open to the storm.

The furious gust that rushed in almost lifted us off our feet. It was indeed a stormy but sternly beautiful night, wildly extraordinary in both its terror and its beauty. A whirlwind seemed to have gathered its strength nearby, for the wind changed direction frequently and violently. The clouds hung so low that they seemed to press on the house’s turrets. Yet their extreme density did not prevent us from seeing the almost living speed with which they rushed from every direction against one another, without moving off into the distance. I repeat that we could see this despite their extreme density. Yet we had no glimpse of the moon or stars, and there were no flashes of lightning. Instead, the undersides of the huge masses of churning vapour, and every object on the ground immediately around us, glowed in an unnatural light. It came from a faintly luminous but clearly visible gaseous vapour that hung around and shrouded the mansion.

“You must not—you shall not look at this!” I said, shuddering, as I led Usher with gentle force from the window to a seat. “These sights that bewilder you are merely electrical phenomena, nothing uncommon. Or perhaps their ghastly source is the foul vapour rising from the lake. Let us close the window. The air is cold and dangerous to your constitution. Here is one of your favourite romances. I’ll read and you shall listen, and we’ll pass this terrible night together.”

The old volume I had picked up was Sir Launcelot Canning’s “Mad Trist”. I had called it one of Usher’s favourites more as a sad joke than in earnest. Its clumsy, unimaginative long-windedness contained little that could interest my friend’s lofty, spiritual imagination. But it was the only book within immediate reach. I vaguely hoped that the very extremity of the nonsense I was about to read might relieve the excitement now agitating the hypochondriac, for the history of mental disorder is full of such strange contradictions. Indeed, if I could judge from the wild, overstrained liveliness with which he listened, or seemed to listen, to the story, I might well have congratulated myself on my plan’s success.

I had reached the well-known part of the story in which Ethelred, the hero of the Trist, has tried in vain to enter the hermit’s home peacefully and decides to force his way in. Here, as readers will remember, the story says:

“And Ethelred, naturally brave at heart and now mighty as well from the strength of the wine he had drunk, waited no longer to negotiate with the hermit, who was indeed stubborn and malicious. Feeling the rain on his shoulders and fearing the growing storm, he raised his mace without hesitation. With blows he quickly made room in the door’s planks for his armoured hand. Pulling hard with it, he cracked and ripped and tore everything apart, until the noise of the dry, hollow-sounding wood rang out alarmingly and echoed through the forest.”

At the end of this sentence, I started and paused for a moment. It seemed to me—though I immediately decided that my excited imagination had deceived me—it seemed to me that from some very distant part of the mansion, I faintly heard what might have been an echo of the exact cracking and ripping sound Sir Launcelot had described so particularly. If an echo, it was certainly muffled and dull. Undoubtedly, only the coincidence had caught my attention. Amid the rattling window frames and the mingled ordinary noises of the still-growing storm, there was surely nothing in the sound itself that should have interested or disturbed me. I continued the story:

“But when the good champion Ethelred entered through the door, he was greatly enraged and amazed to find no sign of the malicious hermit. Instead, an enormous, scaly dragon with a fiery tongue sat guarding a golden palace with a silver floor. On the wall hung a shield of shining brass, bearing this inscription—

Whoever enters here has been a conqueror;
Whoever slays the dragon will win the shield;

And Ethelred raised his mace and struck the dragon’s head. It fell before him and breathed its last foul breath with a shriek so horrible, harsh and piercing that Ethelred had to cover his ears with his hands against the dreadful noise. Nothing like it had ever been heard before.”

Again I stopped abruptly, now in wild amazement. This time there could be no doubt that I had actually heard something, though I could not tell which direction it came from. It was low and apparently distant, but harsh, prolonged and most unusual: a screaming or grating sound, exactly matching the unnatural dragon’s shriek my imagination had already supplied from the author’s description.

This second, extraordinary coincidence overwhelmed me with a thousand conflicting feelings, chiefly wonder and extreme terror. Even so, I retained enough presence of mind to avoid making any remark that might aggravate my companion’s sensitive nerves. I was far from certain that he had noticed these sounds. Yet his manner had certainly changed strangely during the last few minutes. He had gradually turned his chair from facing me to facing the room’s door. I could now see only part of his face, though I noticed his lips trembling as if he were murmuring inaudibly. His head had dropped onto his chest. But a glimpse of his eye in profile, rigidly wide open, told me he was not asleep. His body’s movement contradicted that idea too, for he rocked from side to side with a gentle but constant, even sway. After taking all this in quickly, I resumed Sir Launcelot’s story, which continued:

“And now the champion, having escaped the dragon’s terrible fury, remembered the brass shield and the breaking of the spell upon it. He moved the carcass out of his way and advanced bravely over the castle’s silver floor towards the shield on the wall. But it did not wait for him to reach it. It fell at his feet onto the silver floor with a tremendous, terrible ringing sound.”

No sooner had these words left my lips than I heard a distinct, hollow, metallic clang reverberating, though apparently muffled. It was as if a brass shield had, at that very moment, fallen heavily onto a silver floor. Completely unnerved, I leapt to my feet, but Usher’s measured rocking continued undisturbed. I rushed to his chair. His eyes stared fixedly ahead, and his whole face was rigid as stone. As I put my hand on his shoulder, a violent shudder passed through his entire body. A sickly smile quivered on his lips. I saw that he was speaking in a low, hurried, gibbering murmur, as though unaware I was there. Bending close over him, I finally absorbed the hideous meaning of his words.

“Not hear it? Yes, I hear it, and I have heard it. Long—long—long—many minutes, many hours, many days I have heard it. Yet I dared not—oh, pity me, miserable wretch that I am!—I dared not, I dared not speak! We have put her in the tomb alive! Didn’t I tell you my senses were sharp? Now I tell you I heard her first feeble movements in the hollow coffin. I heard them many, many days ago. Yet I dared not—I dared not speak! And now, tonight—Ethelred—ha! ha!—the breaking of the hermit’s door, the dragon’s death cry, the clang of the shield! Say instead the tearing of her coffin, the scraping of the iron hinges of her prison, and her struggles in the vault’s copper-lined archway! Oh, where can I flee? Won’t she be here soon? Isn’t she hurrying to reproach me for my haste? Haven’t I heard her footsteps on the stairs? Don’t I recognise that heavy, horrible beating of her heart? Madman!” Here he sprang furiously to his feet and shrieked out the words, as though the effort were taking his soul from him. “Madman! I tell you she is standing outside the door this very moment!”

It was as though the superhuman force of his words had acquired the power of a spell. At once, the great old door panels he pointed to slowly threw back their heavy, ebony jaws. The rushing gust had done it. But outside those doors stood the tall, shrouded figure of Lady Madeline of Usher. Blood stained her white robes, and every part of her wasted body showed signs of a bitter struggle. For a moment she stood trembling on the threshold, swaying back and forth. Then, with a low, moaning cry, she fell heavily inwards onto her brother. In her violent and now final death agonies, she bore him to the floor, a corpse, killed by the very terrors he had foreseen.

Aghast, I fled from that room and that mansion. The storm still raged in all its wrath as I crossed the old causeway. Suddenly a wild light shot along the path. I turned to see where such an unusual gleam could have come from, for only the vast house and its shadows were behind me. It was the light of the full, setting, blood-red moon, now shining vividly through the once barely visible crack I have already described, zigzagging from the roof to the base of the building. As I stared, the crack rapidly widened. A fierce breath came from the whirlwind. The moon’s whole disc suddenly burst into view. My brain reeled as I saw the mighty walls rush apart. There came a long, tumultuous shouting sound, like the voice of a thousand waters. And the deep, dank lake at my feet closed sullenly and silently over the fragments of the “House of Usher”.
